prompt: The run of eight workers printed a mean of 124.5 ms. Why is that a poor description of what its users waited?
hint: Look at the line under the table.

choices.text: Only 2 of the 653 requests took a time within 10% of it
choices.why: Right. The mean fell between the quick reads and the slow bookings, where almost nobody was.

choices.text: The mean leaves out the 28 bookings that ended in a 409
choices.why: measure.py averages every request it timed, 409s included.

choices.text: It was computed by the nearest-rank method, like the percentiles
choices.why: Nearest rank is how the percentiles were computed; a mean is a sum divided by a count.

choices.text: Ten seconds is too short a run to compute a mean from
choices.why: 653 values give a perfectly stable mean. The problem is what the mean describes, not how precisely.

prompt: A visit to a page makes 8 requests, and each one independently has a 5% chance of being slower than the p95. In what percentage of visits is at least one request slower than the p95? Round to a whole number.
hint: The chance that all eight stay under it is 0.95 to the eighth power.

prompt: A requirement says the mean response time of the box office must stay under 150 ms. A release makes looks at a show twice as fast and bookings 20% slower. What can happen to the test?
hint: The all row mixes two operations in the proportion the test sent.

choices.text: It fails, because any slower operation fails a mean
choices.why: A mean is a weighted sum; a large gain on the common operation can outweigh a loss on the rare one.

choices.text: It passes while every booking gets slower
choices.why: Right. Four reads in five got faster, so the mean drops, and the requirement says nothing about the slower bookings.

choices.text: Nothing, since a mean of 150 ms already describes the bookings well
choices.why: Bookings took a median of 455.5 ms; the mean of all requests described neither group.

choices.text: It becomes untestable until the p99 is written down as well
choices.why: It stays perfectly testable; it just tests the wrong thing.

prompt: The `all` row printed a p95 of 523.9 ms for 653 requests. Which of these statements follow from that number? Choose every one that does.
hint: A percentile splits the sorted requests into a part under it and a part over it.

choices.text: About 95 of every 100 requests took 523.9 ms or less
choices.why: Yes. That is the definition.

choices.text: Some 30 requests, about one in twenty, took longer than 523.9 ms
choices.why: Yes. 5% of 653 is about 33, and those are the tail the requirement is about.

choices.text: The slowest request took 523.9 ms
choices.why: The slowest took 1071.0 ms; that is the maximum, a different statistic.

choices.text: A typical request took about 523.9 ms
choices.why: The median, 32.0 ms, is the typical request. The p95 describes the slow end.

choices.text: The mean of the run was 95% of 523.9 ms
choices.why: Percentiles and the mean are unrelated computations; the mean was 124.5 ms.

prompt: Twenty response times, sorted, in ms: 18 18 18 18 18 18 19 19 19 20 21 24 32 32 32 37 62 63 64 65. What is their p90 by the nearest-rank method?
Ten response times in ms, in the order they arrived: 12 15 11 40 13 14 90 12 16 13. What is their p90 by the nearest-rank method?
hint: Sort them first. Position 0.9 × 10, counting from 1.

prompt: The same ten response times, 12 15 11 40 13 14 90 12 16 13 ms. What is their mean, in ms?
hint: Add them up and divide by ten.

prompt: A load test of 50 requests reports its p99 by the nearest-rank method. Which request is that?
hint: Work out 0.99 × 50 and round the way the method says.

choices.text: The slowest of the fifty
choices.why: Right. 49.5 rounds up to 50, the last position: with fifty values the p99 is the maximum.

choices.text: The 49th fastest, one place below the slowest
choices.why: That would be rounding down. The method rounds the position up.

choices.text: A value between the two slowest, by interpolation
choices.why: That is k6's definition. Nearest rank always returns a measured value.

choices.text: None: a p99 needs at least 99 requests
choices.why: The method gives an answer for any n; the answer is just the maximum here, which is why it says little.

prompt: In the nearest-rank method the position p/100 × n is rounded ___ to a whole number, so the result is a value that was measured.
A closed generator runs 20 workers, each sending its next request as soon as the last one is answered. The mean response time is 0.25 s. About how many requests a second does the system complete?
hint: Little's law: requests inside the system = throughput × time each spends there.

prompt: In the sweep, going from 8 workers to 32 left throughput near 100 requests a second while the p95 rose from 133.0 to 1214.1 ms. What does that shape say?

choices.text: The generator sent four times as many requests, and the box office answered them all more slowly
choices.why: It sent about the same number per second; that is what a flat throughput means.

choices.text: Something is fully busy, so extra requests wait in a queue
choices.why: Right. X cannot grow, so the extra workers raise R instead.

choices.text: The p95 is unreliable above eight workers and should be ignored
choices.why: Each run had hundreds of requests; the p95 is measuring the queue, which is real.

choices.text: The error rate rose and hid the rest of the throughput
choices.why: The sweep only looked at shows and printed no failures; nothing was hidden.

prompt: k6 reported `http_req_failed` at 3.28% for the random-seat booking test. What were those failures?
hint: Which status at 400 or above can that script receive?

choices.text: Timeouts, because the box office was overloaded
choices.why: A timeout is possible in general, but the run showed a maximum of 1.18 s and the failures disappeared once 409 was declared expected.

choices.text: 409s: random seats somebody already held
choices.why: Right. A correct refusal, which the test should expect.

choices.text: 404s for shows that are no longer on sale
choices.why: The script only picks shows 981 to 1000, which are all on sale.

choices.text: Connections k6 could not open because noConnectionReuse was set
choices.why: A fresh connection per request costs a little time; it does not fail.

prompt: In a load test that books random seats, match each outcome to how the error rate should treat it.
hint: Decide what is expected before the run.

pairs.right: an expected answer, not an error
an error with no status code at all

right_distractors: an error only when the mean is high

prompt: The server was frozen for a whole second, yet the closed run reported a p99 of 5.8 ms. Why?
hint: How many requests did it send during that second?

choices.text: Its clock started at the due time, so the wait was not counted
choices.why: That is the open mode. The closed mode times from when a request is sent.

choices.text: It sent almost nothing while the server was stuck
choices.why: Right. One request waited the second; the rest were never sent. That is coordinated omission.

choices.text: pkill -STOP only slowed the server down instead of stopping it
choices.why: It froze it: the one request in flight took 1007.7 ms.

choices.text: A p99 over 403 requests ignores the slowest four
choices.why: Position 0.99 × 403 rounds up to 399; the four above it are counted in the sample, and only one of them was slow.

prompt: A dashboard stores one p95 per second and shows the mean of the last ten. For the open run that came to 189.4 ms, against 520.0 ms for the whole run. What gives the p95 of the ten seconds?
hint: A percentile is read off one sorted list.

choices.text: The mean of the ten values, weighted by how many requests each second held
choices.why: Weighting fixes a mean of means. A percentile of a union still cannot be built from the parts' percentiles.

choices.text: The largest of the ten per-second values
choices.why: That was 959.3 ms, the p95 of the worst second, which is higher than the p95 of the run.

choices.text: Every timing of the ten seconds, sorted together, read at position 0.95 × n
choices.why: Right. Merge the raw timings, or histograms with the same bins, and compute once.

choices.text: The median of the ten values
choices.why: A median of percentiles is no better than their mean; it would say about 4 ms here.

prompt: Two load generators each ran half of a test. Put the steps for reporting the p95 of the whole test in order.
hint: Nothing is computed until the data is in one place.
items: Keep every raw timing on each generator
Copy both sets of timings into one list
Read the value at position 0.95 × n, rounded up
trap: Averaging the two generators' p95s skips the merge and produces a number that is the p95 of nothing.

prompt: An open generator sends a request every 20 ms and times each from when it was due. The server freezes for exactly one second. The request due 200 ms after the freeze began is answered the moment the server returns, in no time at all. What response time does it record, in ms?
hint: It waits from its due time until the server comes back.

prompt: After a release, the p95 of the booking test fell from 400 ms to 60 ms, and the error rate rose from 0.1% to 12%, all of the new errors 503s answered in about a millisecond. What should the tester report?
hint: Which requests is the new p95 made of?

choices.text: A regression: the server now refuses work quickly, and the latency of successful bookings has to be read apart
choices.why: Right. Fast failures drag the percentiles down; the p95 improved because one request in eight is now a quick refusal.

choices.text: An improvement in latency, and a separate error problem to file
choices.why: The two are one finding: the latency improved because of the errors.

choices.text: Nothing yet, because 12% is within the noise between two runs
choices.why: A move from 0.1% to 12% is two orders of magnitude, far beyond run-to-run noise.

choices.text: A 409 problem, since bookings that fail are seat conflicts
choices.why: These are 503s, which say the server could not serve, not that the seat was taken.

prompt: Generator A reports a p95 of 100 ms over 9,000 requests. Generator B reports a p95 of 900 ms over 1,000 requests of the same test. What is the p95 of all 10,000?
hint: What would you need in hand to compute it?

choices.text: 180 ms, the average weighted by request count
choices.why: Weighting makes a mean of means right; it does not make a mean of percentiles one.

choices.text: 500 ms, the average of the two
choices.why: A plain mean of percentiles is not a percentile of anything.

choices.text: 900 ms, the larger of the two
choices.why: B is a tenth of the requests; the combined p95 could sit well below its p95.

choices.text: It cannot be told from these numbers; merge the timings
choices.why: Right. Only the merged sample, or histograms with the same bins, gives it.
